articles.title: How a Turbocharger Works: Exhaust Power Made Useful
articles.excerpt: A turbocharger uses hot exhaust gas to spin a turbine that pushes extra air into an engine. Learn the parts, the lag, and where the idea came from.
blocks: A turbocharger is a device that uses the engine's own exhaust gas to push more air into its cylinders. More air lets the engine burn more fuel in each cycle, so a small engine can make the power of a larger one. This article explains the parts, why there is sometimes a delay before the power arrives, and where the invention came from.

At its core, a turbocharger is two small fans joined by a shaft. One fan, the **turbine**, sits in the exhaust stream. Hot gas leaving the engine spins it, and according to the Wikipedia article on the subject, turbine speeds can reach as much as 250,000 revolutions per minute.

The other fan, the **compressor**, sits in the air intake. Because it is on the same shaft, it spins whenever the turbine does. It draws in outside air, squeezes it, and feeds it towards the engine. The shaft runs on a bearing inside a centre housing, and a lighter shaft helps the unit respond faster.
Nothing here is driven by the crankshaft. The turbo recovers energy that would otherwise leave through the tailpipe as heat and pressure.
Why more air means more power

An engine makes power by burning fuel with air. Fuel needs a matching amount of oxygen, so the air supply limits how much fuel can be burned usefully. Pushing in compressed air packs more oxygen into the same cylinder volume. The engine control system adds more fuel to match, and each combustion stroke releases more energy.

This is why manufacturers use turbos to fit smaller engines. Explain That Stuff says a well-working turbo may save up to 10 percent of fuel, because a smaller, lighter engine can replace a larger one. A turbo does not create energy from nothing: extra power still needs extra fuel when the driver asks for it.

Squeezing air heats it, and hot air is less dense, which cancels part of the benefit. Many turbocharged engines therefore pass the compressed air through an **intercooler**, a radiator-like unit that cools it before it reaches the cylinders. Cooler air is denser and carries more oxygen.
A turbo can also make more pressure, called boost, than an engine can safely take. A **wastegate** is a valve that lets some exhaust bypass the turbine, which limits the boost.

Turbo lag is the pause between pressing the accelerator and feeling the extra power. The turbine must first be spun up by exhaust gas, and at first there is little of it. A related issue is the boost threshold: at low engine speeds there is not enough exhaust flow to give much boost at all.

Engineers reduce lag in several ways. They make the rotating parts lighter, use twin-scroll or variable-geometry turbines that adjust to the gas flow, or add electric assistance. Explain That Stuff names Garrett's E-Turbo and BorgWarner's eBooster as electrically assisted designs under development.

Lighter turbine and shaft, so it speeds up sooner
Twin-scroll and variable-geometry turbines that adapt to the gas flow
Electric motors that spin the turbo before exhaust flow builds

A supercharger also forces air into the engine, but it is driven by the crankshaft through a belt or gears. It therefore responds immediately, with no lag, but it takes some of the engine's own power to run. A turbocharger uses waste exhaust energy instead, which is why it is often described as more efficient, with a delay as the trade-off.

Forced induction is older than the turbo. According to Wikipedia, Gottlieb Daimler patented a gear-driven air pump in 1885. The turbocharger itself is usually credited to the Swiss engineer Alfred Büchi, who worked at Sulzer and filed a patent in 1905. His first prototype was finished in 1915 and was aimed at aircraft engines that lose power at high altitude, but it was not reliable enough for production.

In 1917 the US National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics tested a turbocharged Liberty L-12 aircraft engine on Pikes Peak, and it showed no power loss up to 4,250 metres. The first commercial turbocharger was delivered in June 1924, and in 1925 Büchi's turbochargers raised the output of a ten-cylinder diesel from 1,300 to 1,860 kilowatts.
For cars, Wikipedia names the 1962 Chevrolet Corvair Monza and the Oldsmobile Jetfire as the first turbocharged production models.

A turbo adds parts, heat and pressure. Explain That Stuff notes that this extra complexity raises maintenance costs and the chance of failure, and that turbocharged engines generally do not last as long. It also cites a 2013 Consumer Reports study which found small turbo engines delivered worse fuel economy than their official figures suggested. The result depends on how the car is driven: asking for boost uses extra fuel.
General information only. Servicing and fuel recommendations vary by engine, so follow the manufacturer's handbook for any particular car.

Turbochargers fit both petrol and diesel engines. Explain That Stuff lists cars, trucks, ships and buses as users. Cummins, which makes diesel engines and turbochargers, also publishes an overview of how the technology works on its own site.

sources.title: How turbochargers work, Explain That Stuff

articles.title: Why Airliners Cruise at About 35,000 Feet
articles.excerpt: Airliners usually cruise between 31,000 and 38,000 feet. See why thin air, engine behaviour and weather make that the sweet spot, and what limits go higher.
blocks: Most passenger jets cruise somewhere between 31,000 and 38,000 feet, which is about 9,400 to 11,600 metres. The short reason is that the air is thinner up there, so the aircraft meets less resistance, while the engines still have enough air to work well. This article lays out the trade-offs that fix the height.
The air gets thinner as you climb

NASA Glenn Research Center explains that air pressure falls with height, because there is less air above to press down. Density, which is how much air is packed into a given volume, falls too. Aircraft designers use a standard atmosphere model for this, since the forces on a wing and body depend directly on air density.

Temperature behaves differently in different layers. In the troposphere, from the ground to about 11,000 metres, it drops steadily with height. In the lower stratosphere, from 11,000 to 25,000 metres, NASA describes it as staying constant. Airliners cruise near the boundary between these layers.

Drag is the air's resistance to a moving object. In thinner air there is less of it. Science ABC says this means the plane needs less fuel and so costs less to run. Thin air also means a wing makes less lift at a given speed, so the aircraft has to fly faster, and that is part of why airliners cruise at high speed rather than slow.

Wikipedia's article on cruising flight puts the balance this way: cruising altitude is where higher ground speed is weighed against falling engine thrust and efficiency at greater heights. There is no single best number, only a compromise.

A jet engine needs air to burn its fuel. The higher the plane flies, the less air each engine swallows, so there is a point where the gain in drag is outweighed by lost engine performance. Science ABC adds that the very cold air, around minus 55 degrees Celsius at cruise height, helps jet engines run efficiently.
A smoother ride above the weather

Most clouds and storms are lower than the usual cruising band. Science ABC says planes up there usually avoid the clouds and turbulence they cause, although they can still fly through weather. The site also lists extra clearance above terrain, fewer bird strikes and more time for pilots to deal with problems as secondary benefits. It mentions a Rüppell's vulture that struck a plane at 37,000 feet in 1973, which shows that birds at that height are rare, not impossible.

Higher flight brings its own problems. Science ABC notes that airliners are certified to about 39,000 to 43,000 feet, and that going beyond the safe limit risks stalling and loss of engine power. It cites the 2004 Pinnacle Airlines Flight 3701 accident as an example. Cabins also have to be pressurised to protect people from the low outside pressure, which is a structural limit.

Climbing costs fuel, so a higher cruise is not always cheaper
Engine thrust and efficiency drop as air thins
A wing must fly faster, or at a higher angle, to carry the same weight
Aircraft have certified altitude limits

The best height is not fixed for a whole journey. As the plane burns fuel it gets lighter, and Wikipedia notes that the altitude giving the best fuel economy rises as weight falls. On long flights, pilots may therefore ask for a step climb to a higher flight level part-way through.
A flight level is the altitude in hundreds of feet, measured with a standard pressure setting. Flight level 350 means 35,000 feet by that convention.
The numbers here are typical ranges from the sources. Each flight's height depends on aircraft type, weight, weather and air traffic control.

Airliners fly high because thin air means less drag, cold air suits jet engines, and the weather is better. They do not fly higher still because engines lose thrust, wings need more speed, and certified limits apply. The usual band of 31,000 to 38,000 feet is where those factors balance.

sources.title: Earth Atmosphere Model, NASA Glenn Research Center
Why Do Airplanes Need To Fly So High?, Science ABC

articles.title: How AI Image Generators Turn Noise Into Pictures
articles.excerpt: Most AI image generators start with random noise and remove it step by step, guided by your text. See the parts: the text encoder, denoiser and decoder.
blocks: Many AI image generators build a picture by starting with random noise and cleaning it up in small steps, guided by the words in your prompt. This approach is called a diffusion model. This article explains the idea in plain terms, and what the main parts of a system such as Stable Diffusion do.

Training starts with a large set of images. According to Wikipedia, each training image is gradually corrupted with random noise over many steps until it is almost pure static. That forward process needs no learning, since adding noise is easy.

The learning happens in the reverse direction. A neural network is trained to undo one small noise step at a time, and in practice it predicts the noise that was added. Wikipedia says the network is typically a U-Net or a transformer. Hugging Face's documentation describes the same idea: at each step the model predicts a noise residual, and a separate scheduler uses it to produce a less noisy image.

To make a new image, the system starts from fresh random noise the size of the target. It then runs the trained network again and again. After each pass the result is a little less noisy, until a picture is left. Hugging Face's example uses 50 steps for a basic model and 25 for its Stable Diffusion walkthrough, though the number is a setting, not a fixed rule.
Because the starting noise is random, a different seed gives a different picture. Using the same seed and settings is what lets a user reproduce a result.

A plain diffusion model produces images that look like its training data, but it does not know what you asked for. Text-to-image systems add a **text encoder**. A tokenizer first splits the prompt into tokens, and the encoder turns them into numbers called embeddings. Wikipedia says commercial generators combine diffusion with text encoders and cross-attention modules, which let the image-making network consult the text as it works.

Hugging Face also describes a setting called guidance scale, which decides how much weight the prompt gets. The pipeline runs the model both with and without the prompt and pushes the result in the direction of the difference. Its example uses a value of 7.5.

Doing all this on full-size images is costly. Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser and Ommer addressed this in a paper first posted in December 2021 and presented at CVPR 2022. They ran diffusion in the compressed space of a pretrained autoencoder, instead of on raw pixels. The paper reports that training powerful pixel-based models can consume hundreds of GPU days, and that working in this latent space cuts the cost while keeping detail.
Stable Diffusion is built this way. According to Hugging Face, it has three separate pretrained models:

A text encoder that turns the prompt into embeddings
A U-Net that removes noise from the compressed picture, guided by the text
A VAE, whose encoder compresses images and whose decoder turns the compressed form back into pixels

In the Hugging Face example, a 512 by 512 image is handled as a latent whose height and width are one eighth of that, because the VAE has three down-sampling layers. The denoising loop works on that small grid, and only at the end does the decoder expand it to the full picture.

Wikipedia says diffusion models were introduced in 2015, drawing on ideas from non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and that a 2020 paper on the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model improved the method. The latent version followed in 2021. Newer systems keep changing the parts; for example, one source notes that Stable Diffusion 3 moved away from the U-Net to a transformer design.
What this explains about the results

The process makes some behaviour easier to understand. The system does not look up and paste pictures. It builds each image from noise using patterns learned in training, so it can produce things that are new but not always correct. Fine details can go wrong because the image is created at a compressed scale first. This is a general description; individual products may differ in architecture and are not all public.
Questions about training data and copyright are separate from how the images are made, and are not covered here.

sources.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models, arXiv
Understanding pipelines, models and schedulers, Hugging Face Diffusers documentation

articles.title: How Noise-Cancelling Headphones Work
articles.excerpt: Active noise cancelling plays a sound that opposes the noise around you. See why it suits engine hum, why speech still gets through, and where it began.
blocks: Noise-cancelling headphones listen to the sound around you and play a mirror-image sound that cancels part of it near your ear. The method is called active noise control. It works best on steady, low-pitched noise such as engine rumble, and less well on sudden or high-pitched sounds.
Sound is a wave, and waves can cancel

Sound is a pressure wave in air. According to Wikipedia, a noise-cancellation speaker emits a wave with the same amplitude but inverted phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other, which is called destructive interference. If the original wave is pushing at a point, the anti-noise wave is pulling, and the sum is close to zero.

FreeCodeCamp describes the system as a real-time loop. Microphones pick up noise, a digital controller works out the cancelling signal, and the speaker plays it. The loop keeps adjusting as conditions change.

Timing is critical. The delay in processing is tiny, but if the anti-noise arrives late, it cannot cancel the original wave properly. The cancellation also happens only in a small zone near the ear canal, not across the room.

**Feedforward** uses a microphone on the outside of the ear cup. It gets a head start on incoming noise but must estimate how long the sound takes to reach the ear.
**Feedback** uses a microphone inside the cup to measure what is left and correct it. It cannot anticipate sudden sounds as well.
**Hybrid** combines both.
Some headphones refine their settings continuously with an adaptive method such as FxLMS, a common algorithm for this job, while others switch between filters prepared in advance.
Where it works and where it does not

Wikipedia says active control works best at low frequencies, and that above about 1,000 hertz the cancelling and reinforcing of sound waves in three-dimensional space becomes unpredictable. Periodic noise, such as engine or propeller noise, is easier to cancel than random noise.

FreeCodeCamp agrees: steady, low-frequency sounds are handled well, while sudden or high-frequency sounds, like claps or speech, are harder. So headphones that cancel an aircraft's drone can still let a conversation through.

Cancelling is only half the design. The ear cups, seals and foam tips also block sound physically, and they are more effective at higher pitches. Wikipedia notes that insulation and mufflers are often enough at higher frequencies. Together, the passive and active parts cover more of the sound range. A broken seal or head movement changes the acoustic path and can reduce the effect unless the system adapts.

Wikipedia traces the idea to Paul Lueg, who received US patent 2,043,416 in 1936 for cancelling tones in ducts and near loudspeakers. In the 1950s, Lawrence J. Fogel patented systems to cancel noise in helicopter and aeroplane cockpits. In 1957, Willard Meeker built a working active earmuff, with a bandwidth of roughly 50 to 500 hertz and about 20 decibels of maximum reduction. The first commercial active noise reduction headsets appeared in the late 1980s.
Why the placement of the speaker matters

Wikipedia explains that where the cancelling speaker sits decides how much power it needs. A speaker placed near the noise source must match that source's power, which is hard for something like a factory fan. A speaker right at the listener's ear needs far less power, but it helps only one person. That trade-off is why headphones are such a natural fit: the speaker is already a few millimetres from the ear canal, and only that small zone has to be quiet.

The same idea of using microphones as a noise reference appears in phones. Wikipedia notes that in mobile phones the microphones farthest from the mouth capture the background noise, and the signal is processed to remove it from the speech. That is noise removal on a call, not anti-noise played into the ear, but it uses the same principle of knowing what the noise looks like.

FreeCodeCamp reports a 2012 study in which people using active noise cancelling in background noise chose listening levels up to 4 decibels lower than with ordinary earbuds. It is one result, and not a promise for every user or product.
Noise cancelling does not give silence. Speech, sharp sounds and sound leaking in through gaps can still be heard, so stay aware of your surroundings, for example near traffic.

articles.title: How a Lift Stays Safe: Brakes, Governors and Rails
articles.excerpt: A lift has several independent safeguards: a counterweight, a spring-applied brake, an overspeed governor and a safety gear that grips the rails.
blocks: A passenger lift (elevator) stays safe because no single part is trusted alone. A counterweight lowers the load on the motor, a brake clamps shut if power is lost, and a separate speed monitor can trigger a grip on the guide rails. This article walks through those layers and the history behind them.

Most tall buildings use traction lifts. Steel or Kevlar ropes pass over a grooved drive wheel, called a sheave, and friction in the grooves provides the grip. Wikipedia says the number of ropes depends on the traction needed, not on the strength of a single rope.

The ropes carry the car on one side and a **counterweight** on the other. Wikipedia says it typically weighs the car plus 40 to 50 percent of the rated load. The motor then only has to move the difference, which cuts the power needed and keeps the car balanced.

The main brake is applied by springs and held open electrically. That design means a power failure does not release it; it closes. This fail-safe approach, where the safe state is the one the system falls back to, appears throughout lift design.

A second layer watches speed. According to the lift equipment maker PFB, an **overspeed governor** detects abnormal speed in the car, and when its tripping speed is exceeded it sends a mechanical signal to the safety gear linkage. Because the signal is mechanical, it does not depend on the lift's electronics working.
The safety gear grips the rails

The **safety gear** is fixed to the car and straddles the steel guide rails that run the height of the shaft. PFB describes it as a roller-type brake that grips the rail and stops the car. It acts on the rails rather than on the ropes, so even a broken rope does not defeat it.

**Instantaneous** gear stops the car abruptly and is listed for rated speeds up to 0.63 metres per second.
**Progressive** gear brakes gradually, which reduces the forces on the car and structure, and is listed for rated speeds up to 2.50 metres per second.

PFB says the European standard EN 81-20 requires the type to match the installation's rated speed and the car's rated load. It also says the gear normally needs no routine maintenance, but recommends a technician inspect it twice a year. These are the maker's figures, and local rules may differ.

Another set of safeguards protects people from the shaft itself. Wikipedia explains that doors prevent riders from falling into, entering or tampering with anything in the shaft. In early manual lifts, interlocks made sure the inner and outer doors were closed before the car could move. Patents for automatic shaft doors followed, including Alexander Miles's in 1887 for doors that block access unless the car is present.
The history: Otis and the broken rope

Early lifts had a real fear attached to them: a snapped rope meant a fall. Elisha Otis introduced a safety lift in the early 1850s that held the platform if its cable broke. Wikipedia dates his public demonstration to 1854 at the New York Crystal Palace.

The New England Historical Society tells it this way: P.T. Barnum offered Otis $100 to demonstrate, and Otis rose on a platform high above a crowd while an assistant cut the cable with an axe. The platform dropped only about two feet, and he told the crowd, "All safe gentlemen, all safe." Sources differ on the details. That article gives both 1853 and 1854 for the event, and other accounts differ about whether it was an axe or a knife.

Both sources agree the first passenger installation was at 488 Broadway in New York. Wikipedia dates it to 23 March 1857. The New England Historical Society says Otis's sons had installed 2,000 Otis elevators within 11 years of his death in 1861.

Not all lifts use ropes over a sheave. Wikipedia says hydraulic lifts push the car up with a cylinder, and are common for buildings of two to five floors, sometimes up to six or eight, at speeds up to 1 metre per second. They are impractical for very tall buildings, where traction lifts are needed.
This is general information. Inspection and testing of any real lift must follow local law and be done by qualified technicians.

sources.title: Lift safety gear: what it is, how it works and how to choose the right one, PFB
Elisha Otis Gets a Sales Lesson From P.T. Barnum, New England Historical Society
